title: the night the Pandavas were away
hookLine: a man wakes to a foot on his chest and asks for one thing, to die by a weapon, and is refused
carry: karma isn't a weapon you aim
tomorrow: the jewel and the guru's son

cards: Dhrishtadyumna is asleep in his tent, on a fine bed, the commander of the Pandava army resting after the war he helped win. He is the man who killed Drona. He wakes because someone is standing on him.
It's Ashvatthama, Drona's son. This is the night the whole book is named for, and the epic tells it without looking away.
Here it's told more gently, holding on to the few moments the text slows down for: a request, a refusal, and a message brought to a dying king.

teach.b: Dhrishtadyumna, pinned down, asks for one thing. In Ganguli's telling he begs to be killed with a weapon, so that he dies as a warrior.
Ashvatthama refuses: a man who killed his teacher, he says in effect, doesn't deserve a warrior's death.
Then he moves through the camp. Others wake and fall: Shikhandi, Uttamaujas, Yudhamanyu, and the five young sons of Draupadi, who came to the war with their fathers.
Kripa and Kritavarma stand at the gate, and fire is set to the camp. Back on the field, Duryodhana hears what they've done, and dies. But the Pandava brothers aren't in the camp.
Neither are Krishna or Satyaki. Earlier that evening, Krishna had taken them to spend the night elsewhere.
The men Ashvatthama most wanted were never there. Now the teaching. Hindus speak of karma: every action bears fruit, as surely as a seed.
Watch the seeds in this war. Drona was brought down with a lie. His son answers with killing in the dark.
And the fruit falls on Draupadi's sons, who did none of it. Ashvatthama thought he was settling an account; he was planting the next one, and tomorrow it comes due for him.
When someone hurts us, it's tempting to say karma will get them, and then to help it along.
The epic's answer is hard and clear: karma isn't a weapon you aim. The moment you aim, the deed is yours, and so is its fruit.

how: Reciters of the Mahabharata tell the night attack as a story of grief and wrongdoing, and the death of Draupadi's sons leads into her demand for justice in the next part of the book.

games.q: you're riding beside Ashvatthama toward the camp. he says the Panchalas' karma has come due, and he's only its tool. what does the teaching say?
o: he's right; karma needs someone's hands.
if he does it, the deed is his, and so is its fruit.
games.why: karma is the fruit of your own action. Ashvatthama's night of revenge became his own account, and tomorrow it comes due.

practice: This is a heavy story, so let the sit be simple. Many Hindus remember the dead by offering water, poured from cupped hands, in a rite called tarpan. Cup your hands in your lap as if they held water.
Bring to mind Draupadi's sons, who were asleep, and anyone you know who is grieving. With a slow breath out, open your hands. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Sauptika. The book of the night attack, where vengeance found Draupadi's sons and missed the men it was meant for.

orig.note: Ashvatthama: Drona's son, who leads the night attack.

carryVoice: Your line: karma isn't a weapon you aim. Tomorrow, a jewel and a mother's grief. That's day eight hundred fifty-three.
